page.h1: HTS Chapter 88: Aircraft, Spacecraft, and Parts Thereof — U.S. Exports & Foreign Tariffs

seo.title: U.S. Aircraft & Spacecraft Exports and Foreign Tariffs (HTS Ch. 88) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: U.S. aircraft and spacecraft exports were $164.33B in 2025, up 22.4%. Where they go, what each country charges on U.S. aircraft and parts, and which tariffs changed since January 2025.

intro:
The U.S. exported **$164.33B** of aircraft, spacecraft and parts in 2025, up **22.4%** on 2024 — the fastest-growing of this report's chapters so far and one of the largest single U.S. export categories. China and France were the two largest buyers, each close to 10% of the total; France's share is mostly engines and other parts (heading 8807) moving through the CFM International (GE/Safran) supply chain that feeds Airbus's own assembly lines, not finished aircraft. Published trade statistics heavily redact individual aircraft and engine sales for confidentiality, so only about **7%** of this chapter's 2025 exports can be matched to a specific HS heading or to a buyer-and-heading pair in official data (see the note under "What the U.S. sells" below); the totals by country and by year are complete and reliable.

For most of the largest buyers, tariffs are not the obstacle: the EU, UK, Canada, Japan, Mexico, Singapore and Brazil all charge **0%** on U.S. aircraft and parts, either under the 1979 WTO Agreement on Trade in Civil Aircraft, a free-trade agreement, or their own exemption. **China** is the one exception — its extra 10% tariff on all U.S. goods reaches finished aircraft and most parts, on top of a low ordinary rate. What usually decides access instead is FAA/EASA-style airworthiness certification, not the tariff schedule.

keyTakeaways: U.S. aircraft and spacecraft exports reached $164.33B in 2025, up 22.4% — the fastest growth of any chapter in this report so far.

Seven of the nine largest buyers (the EU, UK, Canada, Japan, Mexico, Singapore and Brazil) charge 0% on U.S. aircraft and parts, under the WTO Civil Aircraft Agreement, an FTA, or their own exemption; access there turns on airworthiness certification, not tariffs.

China is the exception: its 10% extra tariff on all U.S. goods reaches finished aircraft and most parts, though some imported aviation-maintenance parts may still qualify for China's own duty exemption.
Watch January 10, 2027, when China's 24-point tariff suspension is due to end, and the EU's Boeing/Airbus tariff truce, repeatedly extended since 2021 and due for its next review after July 2026.
